summary.text: Coal is a black or brownish-black sedimentary rock that burns, made mostly of carbon and found in layers called coal seams.
It forms when plants decay into peat, which the heat and pressure of deep burial turn into coal over millions of years.
Coal is used mainly as a fuel, and in 2020 it supplied about a quarter of the world's primary energy and over a third of its electricity.

facts.label: Peak coal-forming periods
facts.value: 90% of coal beds date from the Carboniferous and Permian

facts.label: Biggest consumer
facts.value: China, which mines almost half the world's coal

facts.label: Emissions in 2024
facts.value: Over fifteen billion tonnes of carbon dioxide

items.prompt: Two buried peat bogs end up as different coals: one becomes lignite, the other anthracite. What best explains the difference?

options.label: The lignite bog held a wider mix of plants
The anthracite bog grew from algae, not plants
The anthracite bog reached more heat and pressure
The lignite bog stayed buried for far longer

items.explain: Coal grade depends on the highest temperature and pressure reached during burial: mild conditions give lignite, and the most intense give anthracite.

items.prompt: In an ancient swamp, fallen plants are quickly covered by mud or acidic water before they rot away. Why does this matter for making coal?

options.label: It adds the minerals that make coal black
It speeds the plants' breakdown into gas
It chills the plants so they freeze solid
It shields them from oxidation so peat can form

items.explain: Coalification starts when dead plant matter is protected from oxidation, usually by mud or acidic water, and turns into peat.

items.prompt: One theory explains why so much woody plant matter piled up and became coal in the era when the first trees appeared, instead of rotting. What does it say?

options.label: No animals had yet evolved to eat plants
Fungi and bacteria could not yet break down lignin
The air held too little oxygen for wildfires
Ice sheets froze the forests before they rotted

items.explain: Plants had evolved lignin, which made stems woody, but bacteria and fungi could not yet decompose it, so the wood was buried and turned into coal.

items.prompt: Most of the world's coal beds were laid down during a time of global glaciation. How could an ice age help coal form?

options.label: Lower seas exposed shelves and deltas that became wetlands
Glaciers pressed the peat into coal much faster
Meltwater carried extra carbon into the soil
Glaciers dragged plant debris into deep ocean trenches

items.explain: The glaciation lowered sea level, exposing continental shelves and building wide river deltas, and these large wetlands were ideal for coal formation.

items.prompt: Some coal is found in rock layers older than any land plants. What is it presumed to have come from?

options.label: Remains of early trees
Ash from ancient volcanoes
Shells of sea animals
Remains of algae

items.explain: Coal in Precambrian rock predates land plants, so it is presumed to come from the residues of algae.

items.prompt: People knew about coal for thousands of years, yet used little of it until the Industrial Revolution. What drove the jump in use?

options.label: Miners first learned that it could burn
The invention of the steam engine
Laws banning wood as a fuel
The building of electric power grids

items.explain: Coal use stayed limited until the Industrial Revolution, and with the invention of the steam engine consumption rose.
